capstone: Act as the newly hired information security manager of a fictional 500-employee financial services company with no formal security program. Deliver a management-ready starter kit: (1) a one-page security charter excerpt, (2) an information asset inventory with classifications, (3) a risk register of at least 10 risks with treatment recommendations, (4) a business case for the single highest-priority investment, (5) a metrics dashboard specification, (6) an incident escalation matrix plus a tabletop exercise script, and (7) a 12-month awareness program outline. Present the kit as an executive briefing package with a cover memo explaining sequencing, resource needs, and the top three decisions leadership must make in the first 90 days.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Scenario: The CEO wants the CISO to report to the CIO with no dotted line to the board. As the security manager, what governance risks do you raise and what alternative do you recommend?
Scenario: A business unit launches a customer-facing app without a security review. What governance mechanisms should have caught this, and what management action do you take now?
Self-test: List five elements that belong in a security charter and explain, for each, what management decision it enables.
keyConcepts: Enterprise governance of information and security culture as management responsibilities
Information security strategy as an enabler of business objectives
The security charter: scope, authority, responsibilities, and independence of the security function
Roles and responsibilities: board oversight, executive sponsorship, ownership vs. custodianship
Security policies as management instruments that cascade into standards, baselines, and procedures
Alignment of security strategy to business strategy, risk appetite, and regulatory obligations
labs: Draft a one-page security charter excerpt: write the purpose, authority, responsibilities, and reporting line of the information security function for a fictional mid-size logistics company.
Write three executive-level security objectives that trace from a fictional company's strategic goals (market expansion, customer trust, regulatory compliance) to security outcomes.
Map a RACI matrix for security governance decisions (policy approval, risk acceptance, budget allocation, incident escalation) across board, CEO, CIO, CISO, and business-unit heads.
Draft a short briefing memo to a fictional board explaining why the security function's reporting line matters for independence and oversight.
objectives: Explain why enterprise governance of information is a board-level duty and what a security manager owes senior leadership.
Draft a security charter excerpt that defines the information security function's authority, responsibilities, and reporting lines.
Align a security strategy with organizational mission, risk appetite, and stakeholder expectations.
Differentiate roles and accountability among the board, senior management, data owners, custodians, and the information security manager.
modules.title: Module 1 — Governance Foundations: Culture, Strategy, and the Security Charter

checkpoints: Scenario: Your dashboard shows patch compliance at 99% but mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities is rising. What management questions do you ask, and which metric would you add?
Scenario: The audit committee asks whether the security program is 'good enough.' How do you answer using maturity assessment and metrics rather than opinion?
keyConcepts: Information security governance metrics: KPIs, KRIs, and the difference between activity measures and effectiveness measures
Maturity models and capability assessment as planning tools for program development
Stakeholder identification, analysis, and management for the security function
Security governance frameworks and their role in structuring oversight
Management reporting: translating technical findings into risk-based executive communication
Continuous improvement of governance through audit feedback and lessons learned
labs: Design a metrics dashboard specification: define 6-8 metrics (mix of KPI and KRI) for a fictional retailer, each with definition, data source, reporting frequency, and the management decision it informs.

Perform a self-assessment of a fictional company's program against a five-level maturity scale across governance, risk, program, and incident domains; write a one-paragraph current-state summary per domain.
Build a stakeholder register for a security program rollout: identify at least six stakeholders, their interests, influence, and a tailored communication approach for each.
Write an executive quarterly report template: one-page structure with sections for posture, risks, incidents, metrics trend, and decisions needed.
objectives: Design a metrics dashboard specification that lets senior management evaluate the effectiveness of the security program.
Use maturity and capability models to assess the current state of a security program and plan its development.
Identify security stakeholders, their information needs, and a communication plan that keeps them engaged.
Apply governance frameworks concepts to structure oversight without becoming a compliance-only function.
modules.title: Module 2 — Governance in Practice: Metrics, Maturity, and Stakeholder Management

checkpoints: Scenario: A business owner insists their system is 'low risk' because it was never breached. How do you, as security manager, reframe the discussion around inherent vs. residual risk?
Scenario: Two business units classify the same shared database differently. What management process resolves the conflict, and who owns the decision?
keyConcepts: Information asset identification, classification, and ownership as the foundation of risk management
Threat identification: sources, actors, and emerging technology risks
Vulnerability identification and the role of technical assessment inputs to management
Business impact analysis concepts: linking asset compromise to operational, financial, and reputational consequences
Inherent risk, control effectiveness, and residual risk
Risk scenarios as management communication tools
labs: Build an information asset inventory for a fictional healthcare SaaS startup: list 10+ assets, assign classification tiers, owners, and a one-line business-impact rationale for each.
Write three risk scenarios (threat actor, vulnerability, business consequence) for a fictional financial services firm adopting cloud infrastructure.
Draft an emerging-threats briefing note for senior management: select two current threat trends and explain, in business terms, why each matters to the organization.
Map a sample risk chain from asset through threat and vulnerability to business impact, labeling inherent risk, applied controls, and residual risk.
objectives: Establish a repeatable risk identification process covering assets, threats, vulnerabilities, and business impact.
Lead asset classification and ownership exercises that produce a defensible information asset inventory.
Evaluate emerging threat trends and translate them into risk scenarios relevant to a specific organization.
Distinguish inherent, control, and residual risk and explain their use in management decision-making.
modules.title: Module 3 — Risk Fundamentals: Identifying, Classifying, and Valuing Information Assets and Threats

checkpoints: Scenario: The CFO asks whether a $250K security tool is worth it when 'nothing bad has happened.' Build the management argument using risk treatment and cost-of-breach concepts.
Scenario: A critical risk exceeds the organization's risk appetite but the fix takes nine months. What treatment path do you recommend and how do you document interim acceptance?
keyConcepts: Risk assessment methodologies: qualitative, quantitative, and semi-quantitative approaches
Risk analysis techniques: likelihood and impact estimation, control evaluation
Risk treatment strategies and the risk acceptance process as a management decision
The risk register as the central management artifact: structure, ownership, and lifecycle
Cost-benefit analysis and return on security investment concepts for business cases
Integrating risk assessment into project, procurement, and change decisions
labs: Build a risk register for a fictional e-commerce company: 8-10 risks with description, likelihood, impact, inherent risk, existing controls, residual risk, treatment decision, and owner.
Run a tabletop risk assessment: take one high residual risk from your register and walk through treatment options, writing a one-page recommendation memo with pros, cons, and cost framing for each.
Write a business case for a privileged access management tool: problem statement, risk reduction, cost estimate, alternatives considered, and expected outcomes in executive language.
Draft a risk acceptance memo template: risk description, business justification, compensating controls, review date, and signature block for the accepting authority.
objectives: Run a risk assessment end to end: scope, methodology selection, analysis, and documentation of results.
Build and maintain a risk register that executives can read and act on.
Recommend and justify risk treatment options: mitigate, transfer, accept, or avoid.
Construct a business case for a security investment using cost-benefit and risk-reduction framing.
modules.title: Module 4 — Risk Assessment and Treatment: The Risk Register and the Business Case

checkpoints: Scenario: The board approved strategy but cut the requested budget by 40%. As security manager, how do you reprioritize the roadmap and communicate the resulting residual risk?
Scenario: A vendor proposes a managed detection service to replace two planned hires. What management criteria guide your sourcing recommendation?
keyConcepts: Information security program strategy and its relationship to enterprise strategy
Program resource planning: staffing models, budgeting, and the make-vs-buy decision for security services
Security architecture concepts at the management level: aligning controls to business processes
Policies, standards, baselines, guidelines, and procedures: hierarchy and maintenance
Control selection frameworks and control objectives as management planning inputs
Program roadmaps, milestones, and benefits tracking
labs: Draft a three-year security program roadmap for a fictional manufacturing firm: phases, major initiatives per phase, dependencies, and success criteria for each phase.
Write a staffing plan for a small security team: roles, reporting lines, and which functions to outsource vs. build in-house, with rationale for each sourcing decision.
Draft a policy hierarchy chart: one information security policy statement expanded into three standards and the baselines/procedures beneath them.
Build a program budget outline: categories (people, tools, services, training), a simple allocation across the three-year roadmap, and the assumptions behind it.
objectives: Develop an information security program strategy that operationalizes the security strategy into funded initiatives.
Plan program resources: people, budget, and sourcing models (in-house, outsourced, hybrid).
Design the program's control environment: policies, standards, baselines, and procedures that cascade coherently.
Establish program management practices: roadmaps, milestones, and stakeholder reporting for multi-year initiatives.
modules.title: Module 5 — Building the Program: Strategy, Resources, Standards, and Controls

checkpoints: Scenario: Phishing simulation click rates stay flat after two quarters of training. What management conclusions do you draw and what program changes do you propose?
Scenario: An audit finds the same control deficiency for the third year running. What does this tell you about program management, and what do you change structurally?
keyConcepts: Security awareness programs: design, delivery, and measuring behavior change
Training for specialized roles vs. general workforce awareness
Operational security management: integrating security into change and configuration processes
Third-party and supply-chain risk considerations for the security program
Assurance activities: audits, assessments, penetration tests, and control testing as management inputs
Program performance monitoring and continuous improvement cycles
labs: Design a 12-month awareness program for a fictional insurance company: audience segments, topics per quarter, delivery channels, and two behavior-based success measures.
Write a management response plan for audit findings: template with finding summary, root cause, remediation owner, timeline, and verification step.
Draft a third-party security review checklist for onboarding a new SaaS vendor: ten questions a security manager should ask before contract signature.
Build a quarterly program review agenda: standing items, data inputs, attendees, and the decisions each item is meant to produce.
objectives: Design a security awareness and training program with measurable behavior outcomes, not just completion rates.
Establish operational management practices for the program: change, configuration, and third-party considerations.
Use audit, assessment, and testing results as program inputs that drive prioritized improvement.
Manage program performance through continuous monitoring and periodic review cycles.
modules.title: Module 6 — Running the Program: Awareness, Operations, and Assurance

checkpoints: Scenario: During a suspected data breach, legal wants silence while PR wants a proactive statement. As the security manager leading response, how do you structure the decision and who owns it?
Scenario: The tabletop reveals the backup restoration procedure has never been tested. What management actions follow, and how do you report this gap upward?
keyConcepts: Incident management program components: plans, teams, roles, and responsibilities
Incident classification, prioritization, and escalation criteria
Business continuity and disaster recovery interfaces with incident management
Crisis communication: internal, external, regulatory, and media considerations
Forensics and evidence handling concepts from a management perspective
Post-incident review and lessons-learned integration into the security program
labs: Run a tabletop incident exercise: write a scenario (ransomware at a fictional regional bank), a facilitator script with five injects, discussion questions per inject, and a scoring rubric for the debrief.
Write an incident report template: sections for timeline, impact assessment, containment and eradication actions, communications log, root cause, and corrective actions with owners.
Draft an escalation matrix: incident severity levels, who is notified at each level, decision authority, and target response times.
Write a post-incident lessons-learned action plan: three findings from a fictional incident, each with a corrective action, owner, deadline, and the program change it drives.
objectives: Design an incident management program: plans, roles, escalation criteria, and communication channels.
Lead incident response at the management level: triage, escalation, stakeholder communication, and decision-making under pressure.
Run a tabletop incident exercise that tests plans, people, and decisions rather than tools.
Convert post-incident lessons into program changes: root-cause follow-through and control improvement.
modules.title: Module 7 — Incident Management: Preparation, Response Leadership, and Recovery

objectives: Operate as a security manager, not a technician: translate security needs into business language that executives, boards, and auditors can act on.
Build and defend business cases for security investments using risk quantification, cost-benefit framing, and alignment to organizational strategy.
Design, implement, and govern an enterprise information security program end to end: strategy, policies, standards, controls, and oversight.
Lead risk assessment and treatment cycles, own the risk register, and report residual risk to decision-makers in terms they understand.
Direct incident response at the management level: define escalation criteria, run tabletops, manage communications, and convert lessons learned into program change.
